P01.passage: For centuries the villages of one mountain valley marked the end of the olive harvest with a night procession, led by singers, from the church to the presses. Before 1940 each village sang its own verses to its own tune, and singers from neighboring villages could barely follow one another. From 1950 a regional radio station broadcast one village's procession every harvest night, singers across the valley picked up its words and tune year by year, and by the 1980s the processions in all nine villages used the same verses. Writing in 1990, one folklorist concluded that the changes of the previous fifty years had ______ the custom.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: In the 1920s an amateur naturalist began studying the bluebirds that nested in forty wooden boxes along the fences of her family's farm. Eager to learn how fast the chicks grew, she opened the boxes nearest the house several times a day and lifted the nestlings out to weigh them on a kitchen scale. Within a few weeks a third of those parents had abandoned their boxes, and the boxes far from the house, which she seldom reached, fledged the most young that year. In a review of early bird studies, one biologist called the naturalist's approach ______.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: In 1868 the twenty-four football clubs of a northern county's league, from its towns and villages alike, adopted a new rule for their matches. It forbade carrying the ball in the hands. Eleven of the clubs refused to play under it, left the league, and set up an association of their own that kept the old handling game. By 1880 the county had two codes of football, with separate fixtures, referees, and rulebooks, and a club from one never met a club from the other. Looking back, one sports historian argued that the rule of 1868 had ______ the game.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: In 1974 a state commission published a report on the last dam on the river, which had stood for sixty years. No legislator, newspaper, or fishing club had ever proposed removing it, and the commission had been asked only to price repairs. Its final chapter went further and recommended taking the dam down. Within a year the legislature had held two hearings on removal, and the state's papers had printed hundreds of letters on both sides. In her history of the river, one journalist wrote that the report had ______ the debate over the dam.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. In her last decade, she wrote that almost every new play reminded her of one she had already seen, and her reviews shrank to a paragraph that praised only the rare play she called unlike anything before it. Several plays she dismissed as familiar were praised by younger critics that same season and ran for years. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. Every hull it sold cost a little more than its timber and labor, and the yard kept the difference apart from its own profits. After the storm of 1893 sank fourteen boats, it paid for fourteen new hulls, each handed at no charge to a family that had lost one, and by 1921 every boat lost on that coast had been rebuilt this way. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: For most of the eighteenth century, two towns on opposite banks of a salmon river tore down each other's fish weirs whenever the run was good. In 1790, after two of its boys drowned in a fight on the river, the upstream council declared that its men would cut no more weirs and fined every man who did. The magistrates' books record no weirs cut by upstream men from then until 1815. The downstream council never answered the declaration, and its men went on cutting upstream weirs in most years. Writing a century later, one historian called the truce between the towns from 1790 to 1815 ______.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: In 1952 a state marketing board began buying the reed baskets that households on a small fishing island had woven for generations. Until then each generation of weavers had varied the patterns its parents taught it, so that baskets from 1900 and 1950 look plainly different. The board paid only for baskets that matched, stitch for stitch, the samples in its 1952 pattern book. Households, which still wove for their own boats too, found it simplest to weave every basket to the book, and baskets from 1975 cannot be told from those of 1952. Visiting the island in 1975, one folklorist concluded that the board's purchases had ______ the craft.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The stand had been replanted after a fire in 1988, and the outbreak was a mildew that killed the growing tip of each young oak's main stem every spring. Each tree answered by sending out side branches instead, and by 2019 the surveys measured the oaks at about knee-high, spreading and green, while oaks planted at the same time on an untouched ridge nearby had reached twenty feet. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version the sailor still drowns, and the singers add a closing verse, absent from the printed copies, telling young men that a broken oath will find them out at sea. Several singers told the collectors that this verse was the reason the song was worth singing. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. Driven by a gale, a wall of water a few feet high crossed the valley in less than an hour and drained away by evening, the river back in its old bed by the next morning. Surveyors afterward found every orchard tree and cornstalk lying in the same direction, pointing downstream, still rooted in soil the water had barely disturbed. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. Each sister in turn persuades him to carry messages, move boundary stones, or repeat stories to the neighbors that serve her side of their quarrel. He does whatever the last sister to speak with him asks, and the narrator describes him as content to oblige whoever is paying his wages that week. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. As the city grew, its bakers and brewers came to depend on the wheat and barley from the farms around the town. Each autumn the harvest went south by the trainload to the city's mills, and the town's own population stayed near two thousand through the 1920s, almost all of them farm families and the clerks who weighed and shipped their grain. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: In 1922 two neighboring states signed a treaty dividing the water of a river that crossed both, and much of its later history turned on its seventh clause. That clause fixed each year's shares by the depth of snow at a single mountain stake on one fixed day each spring. A late storm or an early thaw in the days around that date could double or halve a state's share for the whole year, and farmers in both states learned not to plant until that day's reading was announced. Writing in 1980, one legal historian called the seventh clause the treaty's ______.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: In the spring of 1974 a river broke through its levees and flooded some four hundred homes in a farming district. Within a week the ministry had set aside enough money to rebuild every damaged home. To receive any of it, a family had to file a separate claim for each room, attach an estimate from a licensed surveyor, and wait for a regional office to approve the claim, which came back unread if one box was blank; most families were paid the following spring. In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: A weavers' guild built a stone hall beside the market square of a river town in 1580, and the guild was dissolved in 1760. The hall stood on the only ground in the town above the river's high-water mark. Parish records from the wet springs of 1784, 1802 and 1830 list families from the lower streets who lodged in it for weeks at a time, and between those years the council kept its cellars stocked with grain and blankets. In the century after 1760, one historian writes, the hall served chiefly as the town's ______.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: In 1948 a new regional health board took charge of every hospital in a rural county, among them the old stone county hospital. The board had been told to enforce new national standards for wards, staff, and records, and over the next four years its inspectors visited each hospital and closed any that fell short. By 1952 the county hospital, which had kept careful records since 1890, was the only one of the county's five still open, its wards and staff unchanged. Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: For most of the 1960s a retired surgeon sat on the nine-member board of trustees of a county hospital. The hospital depended on a yearly grant from the state health department and on a road the county commissioners maintained to its door. Each spring for the whole decade, the trustees settled in closed session on what to ask of both, and she traveled to the capital and the county seat to present those requests and returned with the officials' terms for the board to debate. In an oral history recorded decades later, one fellow trustee called her the board's ______ during those years.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: From 1951 to 1966 a chemist at a small university laboratory worked with a single technician, a young woman hired straight out of high school. She never touched the apparatus and understood little chemistry. Each evening the chemist described the day's experiments aloud to her as she typed his notes, often stopping mid-sentence to cross out a plan, and he said that only when he explained a step to someone could he see where it would fail. One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: A state forestry service founded in 1911 managed the timber of a mountainous province, and one of its fourteen districts was a narrow valley in the eastern hills. Its farmers had little to do between harvest and spring sowing, the months when felling in other districts most often ran short of hands. Whenever a district fell behind, the service sent to the valley for crews, who were paid by the day and went home when the work was done, and for thirty years most of the province's winter work gangs came from there. One historian argues that, from 1911 to 1940, the valley was above all the service's ______.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: For six centuries a small monastery stood at the top of the only pass between two mountain valleys, each ruled by its own lord. When raiders burned the lowland towns, families from both valleys carried their deeds, seed grain, and church silver up to the monastery, whose walls the raiders never breached. The monks sealed each family's goods in the vaults under its name and handed them back when the family returned, sometimes a generation later, with the seals unbroken. In a history of the pass, one scholar described the monastery as, above all, the region's ______.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: In 2015 a city passed an ordinance limiting where street vendors could park their carts. The city gave its four inspectors no routes or schedules, and they checked carts wherever their other duties happened to take them. Some corners saw an inspector several times a week while others never saw one, and a cart parked in the same spot might be fined on a Tuesday and passed without comment on Friday. Asked about its first year, most of the vendors interviewed for one study described the city's enforcement of the ordinance as ______.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: In 1968 a city opened a new central library, designed by a young architect, on the site of an old train station. The architect placed the main reading room on the top floor, three stories high, under a roof of glass panels set among tiled murals and potted trees. The outer walls were glass from floor to ceiling, and on most days the staff switched on no lamps at all. Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: From 1880 to 1930 the weekly paper of a small river city carried an unsigned column on its front page. Its author reviewed each measure on the city council's agenda in the week before the vote, ending every review with a recommendation. Council minutes show that of the roughly six hundred measures he reviewed in those years, all but a few dozen passed or failed as he had advised, among them the bridge, the waterworks and the new school. One historian of the city calls the column, over the fifty years it ran, the city's ______.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. When the farm failed in 1880, he paid off its debts and sent her a fixed sum every month for the rest of her life. With that money she gave up the village teaching that had left her no hours to write, and nearly all of her published poems date from after 1880. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait, a place with thin soil and almost no trade of its own. Every merchant ship passing through the strait had to anchor under the port's guns and pay a duty on its cargo before going on. The duties, the treasury's ledgers show, paid for the whole of the empire's navy in those waters for most of the century. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: From 1820 to 1860 a mountain village was governed by a council of four elected members, who appointed a secretary to keep the minutes of their meetings. Two members came from the upper hamlet and two from the lower, and on any question that divided the hamlets the council split two to two. The village charter gave the secretary a vote only when the members were evenly divided. The minutes record forty such votes, on the mill, the school, and the new road, and each one settled the matter. In the village's records, one historian has argued, the secretary appears above all as the council's ______.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: Above a harbor town, a river crosses six miles of reedy marsh, and below the marsh the lower river runs past the town's quays to the bay. Water from the river enters the marsh brown with silt and with dye from the mill ditches upstream. The reeds slow it to a crawl, the silt settles among their stems, and the dye binds to the mud. Gauges show as much water leaving the marsh as entering it in every season, and samples taken below the marsh run clear past the quays. One hydrologist has concluded that the marsh serves the lower river as a kind of ______.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: In 1907 a composer built one movement of his first symphony on a folk tune he had heard in a fishing village. The village fiddlers played it as thirty-two bars, repeated for as long as the dancing lasted. The composer kept only the first eight bars, note for note and at the fiddlers' own speed, so that the movement returns again and again to a phrase that never reaches its end. Comparing the symphony with the village version, one critic observed that the composer had ______ the tune.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: In 1871 the hand-loom weavers of a hill district pooled their dues to buy a stone hall in the market town. They spent ten years' dues on carved oak panels and a tall front window, and each autumn hung in it the finest length of cloth from every village. City buyers and visiting tariff officials were walked through the hall before any price or duty was discussed, and the weavers held their own meetings at an inn across the street so that nothing in the hall would look worn. For the next half century, one historian has argued, the hall served the district's weavers chiefly as their ______.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: In 1790 a country surveyor published a map of the kingdom that went through eleven printings in twenty years. Rival maps showed the kingdom's roads and towns as they stood. The surveyor also drew, in dotted lines, a canal joining the kingdom's two great rivers and roads to three hill villages that he expected to grow on water power; the canal dug in 1840 follows his line, and the three villages became the kingdom's chief mill towns. Comparing it with other maps of its day, one historian describes the surveyor's map as, above all, ______.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had long sold their grain. The house never bought or sold a sack of grain itself. At its urging, the forty small dealers who bought from the farmers agreed to bring grain to market on set days in turn, to store it in one shared warehouse, and to send it downriver in a single convoy each month, while every dealer still set his own prices. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: In 1712 a market town ordered every household to send one adult each spring to spend two days clearing the town's drainage ditches, or else to pay a fine of one shilling. As the town spread along the valley, its ditches lengthened from two miles to eleven, while the number of households grew far more slowly. The council raised the duty from two days to nine and the fine from one shilling to ten, and in the 1890s the court heard a steady stream of laborers who could neither spare the days nor pay. By 1900, one historian observes, the ditch rule had become ______.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: From 1878 to 1901 a single inspector examined the cargo landed at a small river port for the customs service. He opened every crate rather than a sample, counted its contents against the ship's papers, and listed even the smallest difference, down to a missing spoon or a bolt of cloth a yard short. Captains complained that unloading at his port took twice as long as at the larger ports on the river, and his successor found the reports accurate to the last item. Reading his reports a century later, one historian described the inspector as ______.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: When a novelist died in 1931, she left the manuscript of her last novel, a story of dockworkers' families set in the 1880s, to her longtime editor. A burst pipe had soaked the trunk it lay in, and many pages had run into gray, blurred sheets. The editor dried and separated them one at a time, had the faded lines photographed under ultraviolet light, and copied out nearly every word. The novel was printed in 1934, with the few lines that could not be read marked by gaps. In a study published decades later, one scholar argued that this editor had ______ the book.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: In 1882 a forty-page pamphlet on the rights of tenant farmers appeared in one rural province, the same year a tenants' movement formed there. Its author, a landowner, argued that tenants already held every right they could fairly claim. The movement's speakers read its sentences aloud at rallies before setting out their own demands against them, and the movement's first written program was arranged under the pamphlet's own chapter headings, each one answered in turn. Looking back, one historian called the pamphlet the movement's ______ in its first decade.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: In 1958 a retired wheat farmer published a memoir of his forty years on the plains, with a chapter for each season of the farm year. Each chapter recounts that season's work, a dry summer or a hard winter, and then closes with several paragraphs telling the reader what the season should teach about thrift, patience, or debt. A chapter about a runaway mule ends the same way, spelling out its lesson for "the young man starting out," whom the author addresses directly throughout the book. Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: In 1928 a record company made the first recording of an old ballad from the hill counties, about a ferryman drowned in a flood. Before then, collectors had written down more than thirty versions of it across the hill counties, with different verses, tunes, and endings. The record sold in every county store. When collectors returned to the same counties in the 1950s, nearly every singer, young or old, sang the record's seven verses to the record's tune, and some apologized that their grandmothers had sung it wrong. One folklorist has argued that the 1928 recording had ______ the ballad.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: From 1884 to 1910 a mining valley's only newspaper was a four-page weekly sold at the pithead for a penny. Miners who believed a foreman had cheated them on the weight of their coal wrote to the paper, which printed every letter as written and mailed bundles of each issue to the state capital and to city dailies. Reporters there reprinted the letters, and in 1893 a legislative committee held hearings on weighing practices, reading several of them aloud. Writing a century later, one historian called the weekly the miners' ______.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: In 1880 a geologist proposed that the hot springs of a mountain basin were fed by rain falling on a ridge to the north. He had reached the idea through a broader theory that the ridge was an old volcano, still warm inside, that heated the rain as it sank. The 1931 survey poured dye into fissures along the ridge and found it in the springs within three weeks. Its boreholes showed the ridge to be cold sandstone throughout, and later textbooks name the ridge as the springs' source without explaining why the water is hot. One historian of geology writes that the 1931 survey ______ the ridge hypothesis.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
